blocks.text: Every time you have worked with a whole column of dates in pandas, that column was really a DatetimeIndex under the hood, and you reached for the dt accessor to pull pieces out of it across every row at once. But a DatetimeIndex is not one solid thing. It is a container built out of many individual moments in time, and each one of those individual moments is its own object with its own name: a Timestamp.

blocks.caption: The same relationship you already know from NumPy, applied to dates. Many scalars make an array, many Timestamps make a DatetimeIndex.

blocks.text: Think back to the NumPy Fundamentals module. A NumPy array is not a special kind of thing on its own, it is a structured collection of individual scalar values, and every operation you run on the array is really happening to each scalar underneath it. A pandas DatetimeIndex works the exact same way. It is a structured collection of individual Timestamp values, and every dt accessor call you have already used in the Date and Time Operations lesson, things like dt.year or dt.dayofweek, is really just running that same logic on every single Timestamp inside the index, one at a time, and handing you back the results as a Series.

This lesson zooms all the way in. Instead of a whole column of a million order dates, you are going to work with exactly one Timestamp at a time: creating it directly, reading its attributes, doing arithmetic on it, comparing it to another Timestamp, and converting it back to a plain Python object when some other library needs that. Everything you learn here is the single value version of what the dt accessor was doing across an entire Series all along.

blocks.caption: Same ideas, smaller scope. This lesson is about the one Timestamp sitting inside every row of that Series.

blocks.text: A Timestamp is pandas own single scalar datetime object, and there are a few common ways to get one. You almost never need to build a DatetimeIndex just to look at one date. If you only care about one specific moment, you build a Timestamp directly.

The most common way to create a Timestamp is to hand pd.Timestamp a string that looks like a date. It parses it and gives you back a real Timestamp object, not just text that happens to look like a date.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

ts = pd.Timestamp('2024-01-15')
ts
# Timestamp('2024-01-15 00:00:00')

type(ts)
# <class 'pandas._libs.tslibs.timestamps.Timestamp'>

blocks.caption: One line turns plain text into an object pandas actually understands as a date.

blocks.title: Timestamp Parsing Can Be Ambiguous Too
blocks.content: pd.Timestamp uses the same parsing rules as pd.to_datetime underneath. A string like 01/02/2024 can be read as January 2nd or February 1st depending on your locale settings. When you are not certain, pass an explicit format string or use an unambiguous format like 2024-01-15 to avoid a silent misread.

blocks.text: When you need to know what time it is right now, not some fixed date you typed in, pd.Timestamp.now() gives you a Timestamp for the current moment, down to microsecond precision.

blocks.caption: You will reach for this constantly for anything involving deadlines, expirations, or overdue checks.

blocks.title: now Versus today
blocks.content: pd.Timestamp.now() includes the current time of day. pd.Timestamp.today() is nearly identical but historically differs slightly around timezone handling. For almost everything in this lesson, now() is the one you want.

blocks.text: Here is the detail that makes Timestamp genuinely convenient rather than just another custom object you have to learn: pd.Timestamp is actually a subclass of Python own built in datetime.datetime. That means almost anywhere in Python that expects a plain datetime.datetime, you can hand it a pandas Timestamp instead and it will just work.

code.content:
import datetime

ts = pd.Timestamp('2024-01-15')
isinstance(ts, datetime.datetime)
# True

blocks.caption: A Timestamp passes isinstance checks against datetime.datetime, so most non pandas code accepts it without complaint.

blocks.title: Almost Everywhere, Not Absolutely Everywhere
blocks.content: Timestamp adds extra precision, like nanoseconds, that plain datetime.datetime cannot represent. A handful of libraries that do a strict type check instead of an isinstance check, or that cannot handle nanosecond precision, will still trip up on a raw Timestamp. That is exactly the case section 7 of this lesson covers.

blocks.text: Every component the dt accessor pulled out of a whole column in the Date and Time Operations lesson, year, month, day, hour, dayofweek, quarter, is available directly on one Timestamp too. There is no accessor needed here, because you are not sitting on top of a Series anymore, you already have the single value in your hand.

code.content:
ts = pd.Timestamp('2024-01-15 09:30:00')

ts.year        # 2024
ts.month       # 1
ts.day         # 15
ts.hour        # 9
ts.dayofweek   # 0  (Monday)
ts.quarter     # 1

blocks.content: {"headers":["Attribute","Returns","Example on 2024-01-15 09:30"],"rows":[[".year","Four digit year","2024"],[".month","1 through 12","1"],[".day","Day of the month, 1 through 31","15"],[".hour","0 through 23","9"],[".dayofweek","0 through 6, Monday is 0","0"],[".quarter","1 through 4","1"]]}

blocks.caption: The exact same components dt.year and dt.month gave you across a whole column, now read straight off one value.

blocks.title: Same Monday Is Zero Convention
blocks.content: ts.dayofweek uses the identical convention as dt.dayofweek on a Series: Monday is 0, Sunday is 6. That consistency is deliberate, it means code you write comparing a single Timestamp against a threshold behaves the same way code comparing a whole column would.

blocks.text: You already saw in the Date and Time Operations lesson that subtracting two datetime columns gives you back a Timedelta, not a plain number. The same rule applies to a single Timestamp. Add or subtract a Timedelta and pandas hands you back a brand new Timestamp, correctly shifted.
4.1 Adding a Timedelta to a Timestamp
This is genuinely useful any time you need to compute a date that is some fixed distance away from a reference point, a deadline that is a week out, or a trial that expires thirty days after signup.

code.content:
reference = pd.Timestamp('2024-01-15')
one_week_later = reference + pd.Timedelta(days=7)
one_week_later
# Timestamp('2024-01-22 00:00:00')

blocks.alt: Adding a Timedelta to a Timestamp
blocks.caption: Add a Timedelta to a Timestamp and pandas hands you back another Timestamp, shifted by exactly that span.

blocks.text: Notice what did not happen here: you did not have to manually track how many days are in January, or worry about a month boundary. pd.Timedelta handles the calendar arithmetic correctly, every time.

Going the other direction, subtracting one Timestamp from another gives you back a Timedelta representing the elapsed span between them, exactly like subtracting two whole datetime columns did, just for a single pair of values instead of a whole Series.

code.content:
signed_up = pd.Timestamp('2024-01-15')
today = pd.Timestamp('2024-03-01')

elapsed = today - signed_up
elapsed
# Timedelta('46 days 00:00:00')

elapsed.days
# 46

blocks.caption: Two single dates in, one elapsed duration out. Same pattern as subtracting two datetime columns, just for one pair of values.

blocks.title: The Result Is a Timedelta, Not an Integer
blocks.content: today minus signed_up gives you a Timedelta object, which carries days, hours, minutes and seconds together. If you only want the whole number of days, pull it out explicitly with .days, exactly the way dt.days worked on a Timedelta Series.

blocks.text: Because a Timestamp behaves like any other ordered value, you can compare two of them directly with the normal comparison operators, less than, greater than, equal to. This is an extremely common real pattern: checking whether a deadline has already passed by comparing it against the current moment.

code.content:
deadline = pd.Timestamp('2024-01-20 17:00:00')
right_now = pd.Timestamp.now()

is_overdue = right_now > deadline
is_overdue
# True

blocks.caption: One comparison, straight answer. This exact pattern shows up everywhere deadlines and expirations need checking.

blocks.title: Naive and Timezone Aware Timestamps Do Not Compare
blocks.content: If one Timestamp carries timezone information and the other does not, comparing them raises a TypeError instead of quietly giving you a wrong answer. Keep both sides of a comparison either both naive or both timezone aware, and convert one with .tz_localize() or .tz_convert() if they do not already match.

blocks.text: Beyond the plain numeric attributes, a Timestamp also exposes a set of boolean checks that answer calendar questions directly, without you having to work out the math yourself. is_month_end and is_month_start are two of the most useful for everyday business logic.

code.content:
ts = pd.Timestamp('2024-01-31')
ts.is_month_end
# True
ts.is_month_start
# False

first_of_feb = pd.Timestamp('2024-02-01')
first_of_feb.is_month_start
# True

blocks.content: {"headers":["Attribute","True when"],"rows":[[".is_month_end","The Timestamp falls on the last calendar day of its month"],[".is_month_start","The Timestamp falls on the first calendar day of its month"]]}

blocks.caption: Two boolean checks that save you from hand rolling month boundary math every time.

blocks.text: These checks are exactly the kind of thing billing systems and reporting pipelines lean on constantly. Flagging the last day of the month to trigger a month end report, or checking is_month_start to know a new billing cycle just began, both come almost for free once you have a Timestamp in hand.

Section 2.3 showed that a Timestamp already passes as a datetime.datetime almost everywhere, thanks to it being a subclass. But every so often you will run into a library that specifically wants the real, plain standard library type, and does not tolerate the extra precision or the subclass. For those cases, .to_pydatetime() converts a Timestamp into an actual datetime.datetime instance.

code.content:
ts = pd.Timestamp('2024-01-15 09:30:00')
plain = ts.to_pydatetime()

type(ts)
# <class 'pandas._libs.tslibs.timestamps.Timestamp'>
type(plain)
# <class 'datetime.datetime'>

blocks.caption: When a library insists on the real standard library type, this is the one line fix.

blocks.title: When You Actually Need This
blocks.content: Most of the time you can hand a Timestamp straight to another library and it will work fine because of the subclass relationship. Reach for to_pydatetime() specifically when you hit an error tied to nanosecond precision, or when a library does a strict type check with type() instead of isinstance() and rejects anything that is not exactly datetime.datetime.

blocks.text: Put everything from this lesson together on a problem you will genuinely run into: a user signs up for a subscription, and you need to compute exactly when it expires, then check whether it already has.

code.content:
signup = pd.Timestamp('2024-01-15 10:00:00')

# a 30 day trial period
trial_length = pd.Timedelta(days=30)
expiration = signup + trial_length
expiration
# Timestamp('2024-02-14 10:00:00')

right_now = pd.Timestamp.now()
has_expired = right_now > expiration
has_expired
# True, if today is past 2024-02-14

blocks.caption: Three ideas from this lesson working together: creation, Timedelta arithmetic, and a direct comparison.

Compute the expiration","signup + pd.Timedelta(days=30)","A new Timestamp exactly 30 days later"],["3. Capture the current moment","pd.Timestamp.now()","A Timestamp for right now"],["4. Compare","right_now > expiration","A plain boolean, expired or not"]]}

blocks.text: Every one of those four steps is something this lesson covered on its own: building a Timestamp from a string, doing Timedelta arithmetic on it, capturing the current moment, and comparing two Timestamps directly. Chained together, they answer a real product question in four lines, no loop and no manual date math anywhere in sight.

items: A Timestamp is the single scalar version of a DatetimeIndex, the same relationship a scalar has to a NumPy array.
Build one from a string with pd.Timestamp(), or capture the current moment with pd.Timestamp.now().
Timestamp is a subclass of Python own datetime.datetime, so it works almost everywhere a plain datetime does.
year, month, day, hour, dayofweek and quarter all read directly off a single Timestamp, no dt accessor required.
Adding a Timedelta shifts a Timestamp forward, subtracting two Timestamps gives you back a Timedelta.
Timestamps compare directly with normal operators, the standard way to check whether something is overdue.
is_month_end and is_month_start answer common billing and reporting questions as plain booleans.
to_pydatetime() converts back to a real standard library datetime.datetime for the rare library that insists on it.

blocks.text: This lesson stayed at the level of one single moment in time. The next lesson in this module, Date Range, builds the other direction, generating an entire sequence of evenly spaced Timestamp objects at once with pd.date_range(), which is exactly how a real DatetimeIndex gets constructed from scratch. Everything you just learned about one Timestamp still applies to every single one of the many Timestamps that sequence will contain.
